Zwettl
TSVET-tel
n. (the Lower Austrian Cistercian abbey of 1138, keeping a Gothic cloister with lavabo and the Bear Skin foundation book)
Middle High German zwetl, from a Slavic root for a clearing or a confluence.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Zwettl in the Waldviertel was founded in 1138 by Hadmar of Kuenring and settled from Heiligenkreuz, and it keeps the most complete Cistercian cloister in Austria, with a Romanesque chapter house and a nine-sided lavabo where the monks washed before meals. Its great treasure is a book: the Bärenhaut or Bear Skin, the abbey's thirteenth-century cartulary, bound in hide and containing the foundation charters, the genealogy of the Kuenrings and the earliest coloured drawings of the family. It has been inhabited since 1138. The dictionary records Zwettl for that habit of writing the title deeds down and keeping them, which is the civil equivalent of a doctrine Scripture states as a command: “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Pro 22:28). The prophetic complaint against a people is that they left marked ways for unmarked ones, “to walk in paths, in a way not cast up” (Jer 18:15), and the exchange is described as trading a spring for a leaking tank, “they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters” (Jer 2:13). Yet a cartulary is not the thing itself, and God tells a religious people what He actually wants kept, “For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice” (Hos 6:6).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a cartulary as a register book of a monastery; a landmark as a mark to designate the boundary of land; a lavatory in this sense is a place for washing; a charter as a written instrument of grant; and a genealogy as an account of descent.

expand to see more

CARTULARY, n. A register book, as of a monastery; a place where papers or records are kept.

LANDMARK, n. Any mark or fixed object by which the limits of a farm or estate may be known and preserved.

LAVATORY, n. A place for washing; a wash-bowl or basin.

CHARTER, n. A written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant or contract.

GENEALOGY, n. An account or history of the descent of a person or family from an ancestor.

Key Scripture

Pro 22:28 — "Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set."

Jer 18:15 — "Because my people hath forgotten me, they have burned incense to vanity, and they have caused them to stumble in their ways from the ancient paths, to walk in paths, in a way not cast up;"

Jer 2:13 — "For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water."

Hos 6:6 — "For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings."

Modern Corruption

Lower Austrian Cistercian abbey of 1138 with Austria's most complete cloister and the thirteenth-century Bear Skin cartulary.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that boundaries written down are a mercy to those who come after. Zwettl bound its charters in hide and kept them for eight hundred years, and the command behind such care is given about field boundaries and holds for every kind, “Remove not the ancient landmark” (Pro 22:28).

The live temptation is to let the register become the religion, which is the characteristic disease of a landed abbey. Jeremiah describes drift as a preference for unmarked roads, “they have caused them to stumble in their ways from the ancient paths” (Jer 18:15), and names the trade as a spring for a cracked cistern, “broken cisterns, that can hold no water” (Jer 2:13). What God says He wants kept is not the parchment, “and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings” (Hos 6:6).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gebul (H1366), a boundary, a landmark; Hebrew shebil (H7635), a path; Hebrew bor (H0877), a cistern, a pit; Hebrew chesed (H2617), mercy, covenant love.

Hebrew gebul (H1366) — a boundary, a border, a landmark; “Remove not the ancient landmark”, Proverbs 22:28.

Hebrew olam (H5769) — long duration, ancient time; “which thy fathers have set”, Proverbs 22:28.

Hebrew shebil (H7635) — a path, a beaten track; “from the ancient paths”, Jeremiah 18:15.

Hebrew maqor (H4726) — a spring, a fountain; “the fountain of living waters”, Jeremiah 2:13.

Hebrew chesed (H2617) — mercy, steadfast covenant love; “For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice”, Hosea 6:6.

Usage

"“Remove not the ancient landmark” (Pro 22:28) — why a cartulary is a kindness."

"“broken cisterns, that can hold no water” (Jer 2:13) — the trade a drifting people makes."

"“For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice” (Hos 6:6) — what God says He wants kept."
